headline: Europe’s Hoax Wave Has Widened, but the Link Is Still Unproven
deck: Flight and newsroom alerts prompted safety responses across Europe, while investigators have not identified a common author.
body: A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted European air traffic on Friday; affected aircraft landed safely and searches found no explosive devices. [E1]
The latest alerts involved at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the United Kingdom. [E2]
Those warnings followed separate Tuesday and Thursday threats that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched. [E3]
Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, its defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said. [E4]
The affected flights had knock-on effects but represented 0.0674% of the 26,709 flights Eurocontrol had scheduled in Europe on Friday. [E5]
In Ireland, a separate set of threats against media organisations disrupted broadcasts and led to staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms. [E6]
Taoiseach Micheál Martin told RTÉ Radio 1, after scheduled broadcasting resumed, that the threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety. [E7]
Martin said European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable. [E8]
The Irish government described the media threats as very serious. [E9]
It said Gardaí were alerted and immediately took necessary precautionary actions with the targeted organisations. [E10]
The government said the first concern in such incidents must be the safety and security of affected people. [E11]
It said hoax threats cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives. [E12]
The statement said it was not yet known whether those responsible were individuals or a centralised or coordinated effort. [E13]
It said the media threats followed similar aviation disruption around Europe and seemed likely to be a coordinated campaign of disruption. [E14]
Gardaí, the Defence Forces, and Irish cyber and aviation authorities were working to establish who was responsible, the government said. [E15]
Gardaí and the Defence Forces were in ongoing liaison with European security counterparts, it said. [E16]
The government said every effort would be made to identify those responsible and hold them to account. [E17]
Its stated priority was keeping people safe despite the unavoidable disruption those steps could cause. [E18]

**The desk's reading.** The sequence now reaches from an alert to flight searches, diversions or escorts, and from an alert to evacuated media workplaces and police searches. That is documented safety disruption across two target sets. Ireland’s assessment that the threats probably form a coordinated campaign is the strongest competing reading, but the same statement says responsibility is unknown; without a public forensic link or identified sender, the record does not establish a common culprit or campaign.

**The next test.** Investigators publicly linking the media and aviation alerts through a sender, delivery infrastructure or other shared technical evidence would support the coordination reading. A finding of different senders or independent origins would support successive anonymous threats; either finding should appear as the authorities’ investigation advances.
